1:
Why the reproof is a song gets the same answer twice. Henry says verse makes it more moving, easier to learn and better handed down, an exposition of the song Moses left behind. Calvin says great events were commonly put into verse so everyone might repeat them, instruction so delivered spreading further than plainer language. Wesley makes it a witness recorded against the hearers, given the prophet and not devised. Henry passes on Jerome's remark that the wellbeloved sang this song in effect when he wept over the city and alluded to it in his own vineyard parable — with the difference that here the fault lies in the vines and there in the husbandmen.

Whose song it is, and to whom, is harder. Gill canvasses three candidates — the Father, Christ, the prophet's people — and settles for one of the first two. Henry has the Father dictating it in honour of the Son, made lord of the vineyard. Ellicott observes the beloved is left unnamed and turns out later to be the LORD. Calvin faces the awkwardness: why should a prophet call God his friend? He rejects as forced the answer that he was a kinsman of Christ, and takes the office of the bridegroom's friend, to whom the bride is entrusted — from which he charges ministers that a man values his wife above his treasures and will sooner hand over his wealth than her, so that to betray such a trust by sloth is the worst wickedness.

Clarke solves the same difficulty textually, reading a song of loves rather than a song of my beloved, since the received text makes the song's author and its addressee the same. Ellicott hears deliberate irony in the opening. The prophet presents himself as a minstrel offering the love-song his hearers enjoyed, and the language recalls the Song of Solomon — the very word for beloved belongs to that book and nowhere else. If the parallel is intentional, he says, it shows how early that poem was read mystically; and he guesses the prophet drew his audience by music, appearing with harp or pipe as others had done.

The vineyard's site is a horn, the son of oil, and no two readers take it alike. Clarke reports Kimchi, that the land is a horn because it stands higher than all lands as a horn stands above the body, and a son of oil because it flows with milk and honey. Ellicott finds an echo of the horn of oil used at anointings and so, on one suggestion, the horn of the anointed, taking the term as an ordinary synonym for a hill, as the Alpine peaks are named. Calvin rejects the reading that makes it Jerusalem's situation, calling it unnatural and forced, and keeps it inside the allegory: vines do better on high ground, as a Latin poet said when he wrote that Bacchus loves the open hills. Wesley says only that hills suit vines.

Clarke will not leave the word alone, surveying how landscape borrows the parts of animals. A promontory is a cape or head, and the Turks call it a nose; the Britons call Cornwall a horn because it narrows to a point. What it most precisely means, he decides on Arabic evidence, is a peak standing by itself, and he ends by describing Tabor, a cone rising alone from a small base and fertile to the summit, suspecting the prophet took his image from it. On the chapter's standing Clarke calls it single and alone, nearest the first in subject but exceeding it in force, severity and elegance. Delitzsch reaches the same conclusion by argument, granting the contacts with the preceding chapters and that the parable grows out of one of them, but holding that a similar date proves nothing against the independence of a piece whose governing idea is its own.
2:
Whether each act of husbandry should be decoded separately is the first disagreement, and it is about method. Ellicott decodes them all: the fence is the law that kept the people distinct, the stones removed the old idolatries, the tower the throne of David or the watchtower the prophets looked from, the winepress the temple where righteousness would issue in wine. The rabbis, he adds, made it a scribe's duty to set a fence about the law. Wesley works the same way later: pruning is the ministers, thorns the people's lusts, withheld rain every blessing lost. Calvin refuses outright, naming the exposition he declines — the fence as the Spirit's protection against the devil, the tower as doctrine, the stones as the annoyances of error. The design was plainer: by unceasing care God did all the best householder could, the order only looking reversed because planting is named after fencing.

The disappointed expectation raises its own difficulty, which Calvin takes up. God is not deceived as a man is, and in the song of Moses he declared beforehand how the people would turn out, so he can no more be mistaken than he can repent. What the verse describes is how they ought to have behaved; and he compares the gospel preached to all, commanded not because obedience is expected but because the mere hearing leaves unbelievers without excuse. Ellicott adds that the wild grapes were sour and hard, no bigger than bilberries, standing for acts of injustice.

When the singer asks his hearers to judge, the manoeuvre is noticed. Ellicott compares Nathan bringing David to sentence himself unawares, the song becoming the text of a discourse in which the beloved speaks through the prophet. Delitzsch says the same from the other side, that the prophet speaks as though he were the beloved, which settles who the beloved must be, and notes a pause before the verdict, the owner breaking a silence that betrays the umpires. Calvin adds that men are made judges in their own cause only where evasion is impossible, which argues the strongest confidence.

What could have been done more admits two senses, and Gill sets them side by side: what further culture could have been given, so nothing remains to add; or what remains to be done by way of punishment, ending in the ruin of the nation as state and church. Ellicott takes the first, cutting off the excuse that the owner was a hard master reaping where he had not sown. Calvin weighs a reading in which the owner reproaches himself for wasted labour, preferring the plainer question. He then faces the hardest objection: could God not have turned their hearts? An idle evasion in their mouths, since conscience holds them and the outward call removes every plea of ignorance; the verse speaks not of what God could do but of what he was under no obligation to do.

The sentence reads as withdrawal, not assault. Ellicott sees the vineyard thrown open as grazing for every enemy of Zion, its distinctness obliterated for a time; Calvin infers backwards that its safety till then was owing to an extraordinary goodness, and lists what God keeps for undoing what he made — cattle to tread it bare, robbers to strip it, drought to kill the root. He turns it on his own day, where a dearth of teaching, or wolves in the church, must be laid to ingratitude. At the close Clarke and Calvin stop on the wordplay, judgment against oppression and righteousness against a cry, pairs sounding alike and meaning opposites; Clarke notes that Kimchi marked it and the rabbis prized such elegance by name, while Calvin observes that a cry is not heard where every man gets what is his own, and defends taking the second table as the test of the first, since where cruelty reigns religion is extinguished.
8:
Ellicott reads the first woe as social history. The series has no precedent in the earlier prophets, he says, and opens with the destruction of the old village life: a nation meant to consist of small proprietors, with the jubilee and the law of heiresses as safeguards, in which might had displaced right. Landmarks were moved, smallholders expelled or killed as Naboth was, the jubilee quietly dropped; large owners rose, often new men, while the dispossessed sank into slavery or tenancy at will. He sets the protest beside the Roman agrarian laws that checked the growth of great estates and beside Latimer's attack on enclosure, adding a conjecture: the last year of Uzziah fell in a jubilee, which may have given the complaint its edge.

The others take the sin, not the system. Calvin insists that buying a field is not wrong in itself and that the disposition is condemned, since greed once inflamed can never be satisfied — whence the saying he quotes from an old preacher, that covetous men would take the sun from the poor if they could. He turns the wish against itself: a man left alone could neither plough nor reap, God having linked men so each needs the others, and the ambitious cannot enjoy renown except in a crowd. Large houses he treats alike, blaming not size but the one occupant filling a building that might hold several families. Henry says much the same, the fault being inordinate desire and carelessness of others, and reaches for a tag: if the whole earth were engrossed, avarice would still thirst. He adds the horseleech's daughters crying Give.

Smaller readings run alongside. Delitzsch supplies the legal background, a law providing for even distribution of the soil and making family holdings inalienable, and parses the tenses so the sentence reaches forward to when the land is all swallowed and no one else left in it. Gill reports two senses of the opening word, a summons on Aben Ezra's account, a groan over punishment on Jarchi's, and passes on Jarchi's count that these woes match in number the psalms' blessings on keepers of the law. Clarke would read the verb in the second person; Wesley states the ambition flatly, that they alone be owners and all others their tenants.

The clause about speaking in the ears divides them. Delitzsch denies the obvious inference, that to say into the ears means softly or secretly, and insists the idiom is for speaking distinctly, so mishearing is impossible; the pointing itself, he notes, softens the boldness by assuming an ellipsis. Clarke calls the sentence imperfect and supplies a verb from the versions. Ellicott agrees no verb stands in the Hebrew but thinks the abruptness the point. Calvin also supplies, taking it that God sits as judge, but makes the broken form deliberate: the threat is an oath cut off before its apodosis, and the incomplete shape holds the hearer in suspense and alarms more than a full sentence would.

What follows curses the returns. Calvin makes the covetous themselves the blight, like creatures whose breath scorches the branches, and notes that men blame the soil when the fault is elsewhere; he sets against the palace-builder a satirist's Alexander, who found the world too narrow and was content at last with a tomb, death alone knowing how small men's bodies are. Ellicott does the arithmetic: a bath is seven and a half gallons, and to get that from ten acres where five hundred might be looked for is a failure like the vine blights or the Irish potato; the seed returns a tenth where thirty and a hundredfold were the rule. Clarke prefers Kimchi's measure, what ten yoke could plough in a day; Gill notes that some read the barrenness as the cause of the empty houses rather than a second stroke, while the Targum makes it the penalty for unpaid tithes.
11:
The second woe falls on drinkers, and Clarke opens with a judgment few would risk: the passage closely resembles one in Amos, who probably wrote earlier, and if this is the copy it hardly equals the original. He then turns philologist on the strong drink, citing two Syrian fathers as unexceptionable witnesses for their country that the word meant palm or date wine. Ellicott widens it to liquor from honey, dates and other fruits, and observes that the offence was as much timing as quantity: morning banquets shocked public feeling and were followed with hardly a break by an evening revel. Gill grants that rising early is healthy and rising to business commendable, so only the day's use is criminal.

What the feast displaced matters more than what it held. Ellicott lists the instruments, preferring lute, cymbal, timbrel and flute to the received names, and calls the life practical atheism: those who live so never see divine order in the world, anticipating in their greed the baser sort of Epicurean. Wesley makes the unregarded work God's recent and threatened judgments. Calvin agrees that music is a science not to be despised and blames only the devotion given it, holding that men so occupied are worse than beasts because they never ask why God created them; and he declines the ingenious expositions of others, naming the one that reads the work of God as Christ.

Why the people go into exile turns on one phrase. Calvin refuses the reading that blames the teachers, charging ignorance gross and voluntary, then faces the objection that many sin knowingly and not by mistake. His answer distinguishes ignorance as occasion from ignorance as cause: men blind themselves under a pretext, or reject the principles by which life should be framed, and are ignorant because they refuse to learn — which does not excuse them, since they bring it on themselves by refusing such a teacher. Ellicott takes the clause more mildly, that they did not foresee what their conduct must come to. On which captivity is meant, Gill rules out the northern deportation as too late for a prophecy of this date, and the fall of Judah too, looking to Rome.

The under-world is then personified, and they differ over how far. Clarke thinks the figure surpasses the parallel in Habakkuk, the grave being brought before our eyes in person, a ravenous monster opening its immeasurable jaws; destruction expects more than a common meal. Ellicott insists the word means not a place of torment but the vast shadow-world of the dead below the earth, only half personified, and notes that the word for glory is the same as that for the honourable men just named, so the original repeats where translation cannot. Calvin takes the soul that Sheol enlarges for its belly, and reads the whole as a device to reach men whom famine had not moved, nobles joined with mean so none may hope to escape.

Who is left grazing divides all five. Delitzsch reads lambs feeding as in their accustomed pasture and nomads eating the waste places of the fat, adding that a land now given to Arab shepherds, with a Mohammedan city on the old site, is a literal fulfilment. Clarke prefers the Greek reading, lambs for strangers, though others read kids, taking the sense to be that luxurious estates become pasture. Ellicott allows the plain reading, oppressed lands turned to common grazing and invaders eating the produce, but offers the possibility that the lambs are the poor set against the fat ones. Calvin makes it a consolation added lest the godly faint, and turns it against the nobles, goats rather than sheep; his strangers are the exiles themselves, so called because their lands had passed to the powerful. Wesley reaches the same more plainly: the strangers are poor Israelites left as vinedressers, strangers only because never the owners.
18:
The cords and cart rope are worked hardest by Clarke, who reports others first. The versions read a long cable, and Houbigant conjectured a word used of something lengthened past its natural measure, yielding sin added to sin until the whole runs to enormous length, like a rope-maker's work as new material is twisted in. To the same effect he quotes Kimchi from the older rabbis, that an evil inclination begins like a fine hair-string and ends like a thick cart-rope, the Aramaic paraphrase reading it likewise.

Then he dissents from all of them. Neither the rabbis nor Lowth, he says, has hit the meaning; the reference seems to be idol sacrifices, the victims decked with gilded horns and hoofs and heads dressed in fillets and garlands. On that reading the cords of vanity are silken strings by which beasts were led, the thicker ropes belonging to the sin-offering, so pride had the upper hand in the acts of humiliation. Ellicott arrives near the same place by another road. He calls the phrase boldly figurative, evil-doers harnessing themselves to the chariot of sin, thinner cords standing for habits and thicker for the stage at which habit is irresistible; and he too suspects an idolatrous procession, a chariot of Baal drawn by worshippers as Cybele's was.

Calvin keeps the cords inward. Vanity means the allurements by which men let themselves be deceived and so harden, whether by laughing at judgment or pleading necessity; and he gives the mechanism precisely. When a man is tempted his conscience asks quietly what he is doing, and sin never advances so freely as not to feel that check, God having provided it so all should not break out into unbridled licence. What men do is flatter themselves that sin is not sin, or lessen it by a pretext, and by these ropes drag themselves on. Wesley reads the cords as lying arguments, the rope as an image of effort. Henry hears false confidence: they think themselves as sure of their design as if hauling it with strong ropes, and will find the cords vanity, breaking under stress. He records a second construction too, that what is dragged is not the sin but its punishment.

The taunt that follows is placed socially and psychologically. Delitzsch identifies the speakers as the free-thinkers of the day, the fools and scorners of the wisdom books, who doubted the day would come and called for what they neither could nor would believe; he distinguishes this carefully from places where the same demand rises from impatience and weak faith rather than contempt. Ellicott hears the actual words of wealthy scoffers, notes that such taunts belong to no one age, and catches the sneer in their use of the title the prophet dwelt on. Henry says the same of the title, adding that they treat the curse as a mere flash and the warnings as bugbears.

Calvin takes the demand apart. Work stands for judgment, since God seems idle while crimes go unpunished, and by punishing he becomes visible in action; the scoffers deny him providence, thinking as Epicurus did that the highest happiness lies in having nothing to do. He writes their speech: let the prophets cry and bawl and hold out their terrors, we shall wait without concern and enjoy ourselves meanwhile. The demand shows the mark dividing two sorts of men — the elect rest on the word and do not despise works, while the ungodly scorn the word though God speak a hundred times and clamour for something to see. Gill makes it the inference of men who took delay for disproof; Wesley notes it was the plain language of their actions. Clarke leaves the theology and hunts a parallel, finding in a late Greek poet the uncommon phrase that the counsel of Jupiter was come, which this verse, he says, exactly explains.
20:
The woe on inverted names draws a fine parallel. Ellicott treats the confusion as the natural product of the sins already named, and sets beside it the historian's account of party spirit in the Peloponnesian war, where rashness was called courage, prudence timidity, treachery cleverness and honesty stupidity; such perversion, he says, is in every age the last outcome of a spirit that neither fears nor loves God. Delitzsch works the three pairs as morally related, not rhetorical: what is hostile to God is dark by nature, and what is sweet to the material taste is bitter to whatever in man is godlike. Calvin reports that some confine the verse to judges and answers that it is general; Wesley keeps both halves, those who justify wicked men and those who condemn the righteous.

The woe on those wise in their own eyes is fitted into a sequence. Delitzsch reads the woes as a chain: doubters of prophecy, then moralists who overturn first principles, then men whose want of humility shuts them out from the wisdom that keeps company with prophecy — and since the next woe concerns justice in the state, he takes this one for the absence of that wisdom in public affairs. Calvin widens it to everyone who, prejudiced in his own favour, refuses to hear God: such men admit they need a bridle and rebel the moment the way is pointed out. Where, he asks, is the man who renounces his own judgment and learns only from God?

The drinkers reappear, and Ellicott marks the change: the earlier revellers were merely self-indulgent, these are the judges themselves, heroes and men of valour only in and for their cups. Delitzsch puts it the same way, renowned not for deciding guilt but for mixing strong wines, and adds that the drink named was not properly wine but an artificial preparation like date wine or cider. Gill sharpens it to valour in the warfare of Bacchus, not of Mars. Calvin answers an objection: bribes are not the only thing that perverts a bench, since favour and hatred blind too, but the prophet named what happens most often, and teachers should attack above all the vices custom has sanctioned.

The tongue of fire sets Clarke going. He takes the figure from a Jewish commentator, wonders so obvious an image is not used oftener, produces the flame that played about a boy's head in Virgil and the volcano there that licks the stars, adds the cloven tongues at Pentecost, and presses the metaphor: fire eats what it meets as a ravenous animal takes prey with its tongue, as Moab said the people would lick up all around like an ox licking grass. Ellicott sees two pictures, a charred field and a tree gone rotten, where the mirth of unjust judges ends. Calvin notices the slide from comparison into metaphor, root and blossom given the nation as to a tree. Delitzsch marks the structure: three woes had been left bare exclamations, but at the unjust judges the threat breaks out and a third therefore joins the two before.

The trembling hills divide the last readers on a point of tense. Clarke refers them to the great earthquake in Uzziah's reign, remembered as an era by two later prophets; Ellicott agrees the shock was still fresh. Delitzsch denies it, holding that the verbs after therefore are prophetic preterites like those before, so the judgment in view is complete and still to come. Calvin takes a third position, granting that the past tense often stands for the future but preferring here punishments already endured, with heavier ones ahead if there is no return. Ellicott renders the carcases as sweepings and thinks famine likelier than plague or war; on the closing refrain he notes its solemn knell-like iteration through the chapters following, bidding the people remember after each woe that this is not all.
26:
Who the signal summons is in dispute. Gill rules out the Chaldeans on two grounds, one nation rather than many and near rather than far, and settles on the Romans, an empire of many nations reaching the ends of the earth. Calvin names the Chaldeans flatly. Delitzsch keeps to neither, holding that the instruments are sought in distant lands and fulfilment began under Ahaz; the passage, he adds, bears every mark of the opposite of a prophecy written after the event, being what an older law had threatened, here in a more plastic form. Clarke leaves identification alone for the whistle, taken from bee-keeping on the authority of two Greek fathers, since keepers draw their bees to the fields and lead them home by a hiss.

The advance is described clause by clause, and they differ on how literally to read it. Clarke reports Kimchi calling the passage a continued exaggeration, and accepts it as hyperbole rightly named: courage keeps them from fatigue, they neither slumber by day nor sleep by night, never ungirding their armour or unlacing their sandals. Delitzsch takes each detail as fact: not one exhausted man drops behind, not one stumbles, since they press on as along a made road; they will not slumber, let alone sleep; and no man has loosened the belt that carries his sword or broken a sandal-lace.

The hoofs draw Clarke's fullest note. Shoeing with iron plates nailed on, he says, is quite modern and unknown to the ancients, as the silence of the Greek and Roman writers proves — especially those on horse medicine, who could not have passed over a matter now so central that a whole science takes its name from it. The silver and gold shoes with which Nero shod his mules cased the whole hoof and were tied on, so a hoof's natural firmness mattered far more then than now; he cites Xenophon that a good one is hard and hollow and rings like a cymbal. Delitzsch adds a point about the bows: their length equalled a man's height, so the string was trodden with the left foot, and that they are trodden already shows the enemy near.

The roaring is heard in two stages. Delitzsch distinguishes the cry of a lion eager for prey from the growl it makes when gathering to spring, and hears in the army first the war-shout and then an ominous murmur; the poetic name used, he notes, belongs properly to the male. Calvin takes the comparison morally: these are not men moved by compassion but savage beasts, their strength necessary so a wayward people should learn at last that it had to do not with men but with God, into whose hands it is a fearful thing to fall. Gill hears the sound of a beast just seizing its prey.

The last verse turns the roar into surf, then into darkness. Delitzsch makes the enemy subject and Judah object, a nation overwhelmed as by a sea, which looking to its own land finds darkness where its cheerfulness had been. Calvin denies the attack is accidental, calls it a deluge in which the country suffers shipwreck, and closes with men casting their eyes up and down for a way out and finding none: we may escape the hand of men, he says, but how escape the hand of God? Ellicott hears in the same word the shout and tramp of armies, which suggests the sea, and the sea the darkness of a tempest, or an earthquake, or an eclipse; he would read clouds rather than heavens. Wesley takes the second noun to explain the first, so the darkness is sorrow. Clarke ends on the text, assembling the Greek editions, the Arabic and a second-century Coptic version to argue that the original had them looking to the heavens above as well as the earth beneath.
